title: Widget systems
description: Widget systems compose dashboards from independent components: each widget declares its data needs, renders itself, and handles its own refresh. The host provides the grid, the data bus, and the lifecycle. Widgets are sandboxed plugins — a crashing widget shows an error card, not a broken dashboard. The catalog (gallery of available widgets) is the discovery surface.
mechanism: Widget = {data query, render, refresh policy, config schema}. Host: grid layout + data bus + lifecycle + error boundaries. Catalog for discovery.
algo: O(widgets) render; independent refresh per widget.

title: Drag-drop dashboard layout
description: Dashboard layout is drag-drop: widgets move, resize, and snap to the grid; the layout persists per user. The grid is 12 columns (responsive breakpoints collapse it); resize handles adjust spans; collision resolution pushes widgets down. The layout model is simple — {x, y, w, h} per widget — and everything else is interaction polish.
mechanism: Grid state: widgets with {x,y,w,h}; drag updates position (snap); resize updates spans; collisions resolved by pushing; persist per user; breakpoints reflow.

title: Grid systems
description: Dashboard grids are responsive: 12 columns on desktop, fewer on tablet, one on phone; widgets reflow (not just shrink) at each breakpoint. The breakpoint map is per-widget ({desktop: {x,y,w,h}, mobile: ...}) or automatic (stack in order). Reflow must be predictable — the widget order never changes, only the arrangement.
mechanism: Breakpoints: >=1200 (12 cols), >=768 (6), else 1. Per-widget layouts per breakpoint or auto-stack. Order stable across breakpoints.

title: Dashboard data binding
description: Data binding connects widgets to queries: each widget declares a query (SQL, PromQL, API), the host executes on the refresh schedule, and results flow to the renderer. Binding is declarative — the widget says WHAT, the host handles WHEN and HOW (caching, batching, retries). Time ranges are global: one picker drives every widget's query window.
mechanism: Widget declares query + refresh; host schedules, caches, batches; global time range injected into queries. Loading/error states per widget.
algo: O(widgets) queries per refresh; batching and caching cut it.
demo:
# declarative binding: widget says WHAT; host handles WHEN/HOW
queries = {
    'cpu': 'avg(cpu_usage)',
    'errors': 'sum(errors)',
}
cache = {}

def refresh(widget, time_range):
    key = (widget, time_range)
    if key not in cache:  # host: cache + batch + retry
        cache[key] = '<result of %s over %s>' % (queries[widget], time_range)
    return cache[key]

print(refresh('cpu', 'last 1h'))
print(refresh('cpu', 'last 1h'), '(cached: host dedups identical queries)')
print('global time picker -> injected into every widget query')

title: Refresh policies
description: Refresh policies balance freshness against cost: real-time (streaming), interval (5s/30s/5m), manual, and on-event. Each widget picks its policy; the host enforces minimums (no 100ms refresh on a heavy query) and pauses offscreen widgets. Stale indicators show data age — a dashboard that silently shows old data lies.
mechanism: Per-widget policy; host minimums by query cost; visibility pause; stale badges (data age). Manual refresh always available.
algo: O(visible widgets) per tick; paused offscreen.
demo:
import time

widgets = [
    {'name': 'cpu', 'policy': 5, 'last': 0, 'visible': True},
    {'name': 'deploy', 'policy': 'manual', 'last': 0, 'visible': True},
    {'name': 'hidden', 'policy': 5, 'last': 0, 'visible': False},
]
now = 100
for w in widgets:
    due = w['visible'] and w['policy'] != 'manual' and now - w['last'] >= w['policy']
    age = now - w['last']
    stale = ' STALE (%ds old)' % age if age > (w['policy'] if isinstance(w['policy'], int) else 60) else ''
    print('%-7s refresh=%s -> %s%s' % (w['name'], w['policy'], 'FETCH' if due else 'skip', stale))
print('offscreen paused; stale badges: never silently show old data')

title: Drill-down
description: Drill-down navigates from summary to detail: click a chart segment to filter the whole dashboard to it, click again to go deeper (region -> datacenter -> host). The dashboard state becomes a filter stack; breadcrumbs navigate back. Every widget respects the global filters — drill-down is a dashboard-wide operation, not per-widget.
mechanism: Click -> add filter to the global stack -> all widgets re-query with filters -> breadcrumb shows the path. Esc pops the stack.
algo: O(widgets) re-query per drill; filter stack O(depth).
demo:
# filter stack: every widget re-queries with the global filters
filters = []

def drill(dimension, value):
    filters.append((dimension, value))
    print('drill: %s=%s -> all widgets re-query %s' % (dimension, value, filters))

def back():
    f = filters.pop()
    print('back: removed %s (breadcrumb)' % (f,))

drill('region', 'us-east'); drill('host', 'web-3')
back()
print('dashboard-wide: one filter stack, every widget respects it')

title: Saved views
description: Saved views capture the dashboard state — layout, filters, time range — as a named, shareable snapshot. Users save their investigations ('the outage view') and return in one click. Views are versioned with the dashboard (a view referencing a deleted widget degrades gracefully). Personal views vs shared views: the sharing model decides.
mechanism: Serialize {layout, filters, time range, widget config} with a name; version against the dashboard schema; graceful degradation for missing widgets. Personal/team scopes.
demo:
import json

view = {'name': 'outage-view', 'v': 1, 'layout': ['cpu', 'errors'],
        'filters': [('region', 'us-east')], 'range': 'last 6h'}
saved = json.dumps(view)

def load(s, current_widgets):
    v = json.loads(s)
    alive = [w for w in v['layout'] if w in current_widgets]  # graceful degrade
    dropped = set(v['layout']) - set(alive)
    return alive, dropped

print('loaded:', load(saved, {'cpu', 'memory'}))
print('deleted widgets degrade gracefully; views versioned with the dashboard')

title: Sharing dashboards

title: Dashboard theming
description: Dashboard theming keeps widgets consistent: the theme tokens (this lane's high-contrast database) flow into every widget — chart colors from the palette, text from tokens, dark mode everywhere. Chart palettes are colorblind-safe sequences, not rainbows. Widgets never hardcode colors; the host injects the theme.
mechanism: Host provides theme context to widgets; chart palettes from the token system; per-widget theme override (rare). Forced-colors respected.
demo:
# host injects theme; widgets never hardcode colors
theme = {'bg': '#121212', 'text': '#f0f0f0',
         'palette': ['#56B4E9', '#E69F00', '#009E73']}  # colorblind-safe

def render_chart(series, theme):
    colors = [theme['palette'][i % len(theme['palette'])] for i in range(len(series))]
    return list(zip(series, colors))

print(render_chart(['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'], theme))
print('palette cycles colorblind-safe; dark mode via tokens; no hardcoded colors')

title: Responsive dashboards
description: Responsive dashboards reflow, not just shrink: the 12-column grid collapses to stacked cards on phones, charts switch to simplified forms, and tables become lists. The mobile dashboard is often a different product — the 3 key numbers, not the 30 widgets. Design the breakpoints deliberately; test on real phones.
mechanism: Breakpoints reflow the grid; widget variants per breakpoint (chart -> stat); tables -> cards. Mobile shows the key widgets first (priority order).
demo:
widgets = [
    {'name': 'revenue', 'priority': 1, 'mobile': 'stat'},
    {'name': 'chart30d', 'priority': 2, 'mobile': 'mini-chart'},
    {'name': 'fulltable', 'priority': 5, 'mobile': 'hidden'},
]

def mobile_view(ws):
    return [(w['name'], w['mobile']) for w in sorted(ws, key=lambda w: w['priority'])
            if w['mobile'] != 'hidden']

print('desktop: all 3 widgets, 12-col grid')
print('mobile :', mobile_view(widgets), '(priority order, simplified forms)')
print('mobile dashboard = the 3 key numbers, not 30 shrunken widgets')

title: Dashboard performance
description: Dashboard performance is query performance: N widgets x M queries per refresh = the load. The fixes are batching (one query serving many widgets), caching (shared results), virtualization (offscreen widgets don't query), and query budgets (slow queries get killed, not waited on). The dashboard loads in under 2s or users stop trusting it.
mechanism: Batch identical queries; cache by (query, range); virtualize offscreen; kill slow queries (timeout + error card); progressive load (key widgets first).
algo: O(unique queries), not O(widgets); budgets enforced.
provenance: Public-harvest: curated from public technical literature, documentation, and established engineering practice.

title: Dashboard access control
description: Dashboard access control is per-widget, not just per-dashboard: revenue numbers visible to execs, hidden from contractors — on the same dashboard. The model is roles -> widgets (and row-level filters in queries). Hidden widgets don't just hide the UI; the query never runs for unauthorized users (no data in the network tab).
mechanism: Role-based widget visibility; queries parameterized by role (row filters); server-side enforcement (never rely on UI hiding). Audit who saw what.
algo: O(1) per widget check; enforcement server-side.

title: Dashboard export
description: Dashboard export serves the workflows dashboards don't: PDF reports for meetings, PNG snapshots for incident timelines, CSV of the underlying data for analysis. title: Real-time dashboards
description: Real-time dashboards stream: WebSocket/SSE pushes updates, widgets patch in place (no full re-render), and the data pipeline is stream-first (Kafka -> processing -> push). The challenges are backpressure (slow client?), ordering (late events), and cost (every user x every update). Real-time is a spectrum — 1s updates for trading, 30s for ops — pick deliberately.
mechanism: Stream bus (WS/SSE) -> per-widget patch updates -> chart append (not redraw). Backpressure: drop to snapshots. Late events: watermark + correct.
algo: O(updates) patches; backpressure policy decides overload behavior.
demo:
# patch in place: append points, never full re-render
series = [1, 2, 3]

def on_tick(value):
    series.append(value)      # chart: append point
    if len(series) > 100:
        del series[0]         # windowed: drop old
    return 'patched (no re-render)'

for v in (4, 5, 6):
    print('tick %d -> %s, window=%s' % (v, on_tick(v), series[-3:]))
print('backpressure: slow client -> snapshots, not every tick')
print('real-time is a spectrum: 1s trading, 30s ops -- pick deliberately')
